fields.headline: Who Reacts, Who Doesn't
fields.subhead: Helium, neon, and argon barely react with anything. Sodium and chlorine react easily.
fields.keyq: What is different about the electrons in He, Ne, and Ar?

imageSubjects.concept: a row of glowing noble gas discharge tubes against a dark background

slides.notes: Hook. Ask first, answer later. Do not say 'want' or 'need' of atoms; describe outcomes. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a row of glowing noble gas discharge tubes against a dark background.

fields.headline: Three Words You Need First
fields.subhead: Write these before we go further. Everything after this slide uses them.
fields.k1_b: An electron in the outermost energy level.
fields.k2_b: An electron in an inner, filled energy level.
fields.k3_b: Outer s and p sublevels full: 2 or 8 electrons.
fields.mustwrite: Valence electrons are the electrons in the outermost energy level, the one with the highest n.

imageSubjects.aside: a worn chemistry notebook open to a hand-ruled page

slides.notes: Students write the three terms. Noble gas configuration = outer s and p sublevels full (2 for He, 8 for the rest); say 'full' means s and p, not the whole shell. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a worn chemistry notebook open to a hand-ruled page.

fields.headline: Core or Valence? Find the Highest n
fields.subhead: Chlorine has 17 electrons. Only the ones in n = 3 are valence.
fields.a1_b: 1s^{2} 2s^{2} 2p^{6} fill n = 1 and n = 2. That is 10 electrons.
fields.a2_b: 3s^{2} 3p^{5} is the highest level, n = 3. That is 7 electrons.

slides.notes: Cl: 10 core + 7 valence = 17. Valence = highest n only. Figure shows the split.

fields.headline: Valence Electrons From the Table
fields.subhead: For main-group elements, the group number gives you the count.
fields.a1_b:
Groups 1 and 2: the group number.
Groups 13 to 18: the units digit.
fields.a2_b: Helium is in group 18 and has 2 valence electrons, not 8.
fields.a3_b: Groups 3 to 12, the transition metals. Their ions follow the rule on slide 13.

slides.notes: Main-group only. PROVISIONAL: transition-metal valence counting is deliberately left out (brief slide 6; Matt to decide whether d electrons count). Say only that their ions lose the outer s electrons first (slide 13). Lewis dot preview omitted: belongs to a later unit (S5.1), PROVISIONAL.

fields.headline: Example: Valence Electrons of P and Ca
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: Use each configuration to find the number of valence electrons in phosphorus and calcium.
fields.g2_b:
Highest n for each
Valence electron count
Check against the group
fields.mustwrite: Valence electrons are the s and p electrons in the highest n only.

imageSubjects.aside: a block of red phosphorus beside a piece of calcium metal

slides.notes: Worked example, do together. Answers on next slide. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a block of red phosphorus beside a piece of calcium metal.

fields.headline: Phosphorus and Calcium, Worked
fields.subhead: Check the group number last. It should agree with your count.
fields.f1_b:
Find the highest n.
Count every electron in it.
fields.mustwrite: P has 5 valence electrons (group 15). Ca has 2 (group 2).

imageSubjects.data: a pencil resting on a page of handwritten configurations

slides.notes: P: n = 3, 3s2 3p3 = 5. Ca: n = 4, 4s2 = 2. Both agree with group number. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a pencil resting on a page of handwritten configurations.

fields.headline: Why Noble Gases Barely React
fields.subhead: Look at the outer s and p sublevels of each one.
fields.a1_b: Ne, Ar, and Kr have 8 electrons in their outer s and p sublevels. Helium has 2.
fields.a2_b: Full means s and p. Argon's 3d sublevel is empty, so n = 3 is not completely full.
fields.a3_b: Later in this section we compare ions to these four configurations.

slides.notes: Full means outer s and p. Argon's 3d is empty, so n = 3 is not completely full; this fixes the 'full shell = 8' misconception. Avoid personifying atoms.

fields.headline: What Makes an Ion
fields.subhead: Atoms become ions by gaining or losing electrons. The nucleus does not change.
fields.c1_b:
Loses electrons.
Positive charge.
Na → Na^{+}: 11 electrons become 10.
Charge: 1+
fields.c2_b:
Gains electrons.
Negative charge.
Cl → Cl^{−}: 17 electrons become 18.
Charge: 1−
fields.mustwrite: Electrons = atomic number − charge. Protons never change.

imageSubjects.concept: a bowl of table salt crystals on dark slate

slides.notes: Electrons = atomic number minus charge. Protons never change. Here we only describe what an ion is; the charge-prediction rule comes at the end of the section (slide 18). Anion charge is also written plain (1−) because the superscript minus is faint. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a bowl of table salt crystals on dark slate.

fields.headline: Na Loses One, Cl Gains One
fields.subhead: Electrons leave from the highest n first. A gained electron fills the open 3p spot.
fields.a2_b:
One electron fills 3p: 17 → 18.
Cl^{−}: charge 1−. Matches [Ar].

slides.notes: MERGED slide (was two: Na+ orbitals and Cl- orbitals). Na loses its 3s1, leaving the neon configuration; Cl's added electron goes into the open 3p spot, not a new level, and matches argon. Click build replaces the static figure: sodium builds first, then the chlorine build covers it in the same slot (the 20-content-slide cap leaves no room for a second slide). The state line under each diagram gives the plain, large charge so the minus is legible. The static PNG chem_u02_s2.4_na_cl_ions.png stays on disk for print. Do not yet say why these charges: the rule comes at the end of the section.

fields.headline: Three More Ions, Same Move
fields.subhead: Remove from the highest n, or fill the open spots in s and p.
fields.mustwrite: A cation loses from the highest n. An anion fills open spots in s and p.

imageSubjects.aside: a sealed ampoule of dark red-brown liquid bromine in a rack

slides.notes: MERGED slide (was two card slides: Mg2+/Al3+/Ca2+ and O2-/S2-/Br-). Mg2+ and Ca2+ now appear in the Ca walk-through and the worked example; S2- in the worked example. Br keeps its full 3d10. Charge lines are plain so anion minus signs are legible. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a sealed ampoule of dark red-brown liquid bromine in a rack.

fields.headline: Same Electrons, Different Atoms
fields.subhead: Isoelectronic means the same number of electrons and the same configuration.
fields.a2_b: The proton counts differ, so these are different particles. Their sizes differ too. Unit 3 explains why.
fields.a3_b: Electrons = protons − charge. Check any column.

slides.notes: Isoelectronic = same electron count and configuration. Sizes differ; the reason is Unit 3, only pointed to here (one-line pointer, not taught).

fields.headline: Transition Metal Ions: 4s Leaves First
fields.subhead: This is the rule that surprises people. Watch the order.
fields.c1_b:
Remove electrons from the outermost s first: 4s.

Then take from 3d if more must go.
fields.c2_b:
Once 3d has electrons, it sits lower in energy than 4s.

So 4s electrons leave first, even though 4s filled first.
fields.mustwrite: Transition-metal ions lose their ns electrons before their (n−1)d electrons.

imageSubjects.concept: a polished iron nail and a copper coin on dark slate

slides.notes: PROVISIONAL (simplified): 'why 4s leaves first' is a student-language account (once 3d has electrons it sits lower than 4s). It is not a full energetics explanation; do not extend it. Matches S2.3 wording. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a polished iron nail and a copper coin on dark slate.

fields.headline: Iron: Fe, Fe^{2+}, and Fe^{3+}
fields.subhead: Both 4s electrons go first. The third comes out of 3d.

slides.notes: Fe 26, Fe2+ 24 [Ar]3d6, Fe3+ 23 [Ar]3d5. Present 3d5 as an observed electron count, not proof of a cause. Click build replaces the static figure: one slide carries Fe, Fe2+ and Fe3+ (the 4s arrows leave first, then one 3d). The static PNG chem_u02_s2.4_fe_ions_orbitals.png stays on disk for print.

fields.headline: Example: Zn^{2+}, Cu^{+}, and Cu^{2+}
fields.subhead: Same rule as iron. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: Write the [Ar] shorthand for Zn^{2+}, Cu^{+}, and Cu^{2+}.
fields.g2_b:
Electrons to remove
Which sublevel they leave
Each ion's shorthand
fields.mustwrite: Take the 4s electrons first. Only then take from 3d.

imageSubjects.aside: a galvanized zinc sheet beside a length of copper wire

slides.notes: Same rule as iron. Cu is the taught exception: [Ar] 4s1 3d10. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a galvanized zinc sheet beside a length of copper wire.

fields.headline: Zn^{2+}, Cu^{+}, and Cu^{2+}, Worked
fields.subhead: None of these ends at a noble gas configuration.
fields.f1_b:
Take 4s first, then 3d.
Zn 30 → 28. Cu 29 → 28 or 27.
fields.mustwrite: Zn^{2+} and Cu^{+} are both [Ar] 3d^{10}. Cu^{2+} is [Ar] 3d^{9}.

imageSubjects.data: a pencil resting on a page of handwritten calculations

slides.notes: Zn2+ = Cu+ = [Ar] 3d10 (28 e). Cu2+ = [Ar] 3d9 (27 e). Not noble-gas configurations; these are stable anyway. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: a pencil resting on a page of handwritten calculations.

fields.headline: Why Calcium Forms Ca^{2+}
fields.subhead: Count valence electrons first. The count tells you the move.
fields.c2_b:
Lose both 4s electrons: [Ar].
18 electrons, 20 protons.
Charge: 20 − 18 = 2+
fields.mustwrite: Ca has 2 valence electrons. Losing both leaves [Ar], so Ca forms Ca^{2+}.

slides.notes: NEW. Closing synthesis, step 1: Ca walk-through in four moves: count (2 valence), move (lose 2; gaining 6 is more), result ([Ar], 18 electrons), charge (20 protons minus 18 electrons = 2+). Valence-electron reasoning only. Do not teach ionization energy; Unit 3 (U3.4, U3.7) explains the energy side. Scope boundary set by Matt 2026-10-04; DECISIONS.md not changed. Avoid 'wants' or 'needs' language for atoms. The picture slot holds the Ca click build (valence arrows highlighted, then removed one per click).

fields.headline: Valence Electrons Predict the Charge
fields.subhead: Lose or gain the fewest electrons to reach 8. Unit 3 will explain the energy side.
fields.a1_b:
Groups 1, 2, 13 lose all their valence electrons.
Charges 1+, 2+, 3+.
fields.a3_b: Group 14 and the transition metals. Group 18 is already full.

slides.notes: NEW. Rule by group (period 3 examples; hand-built, every count asserted in the figure script). Main group: lose or gain the fewest electrons to reach 8 (2 in period 1). PROVISIONAL: group 14 (4 lost or 4 gained, no 'fewest') and the transition metals are not predicted by this rule here; transition-metal ions were covered on the iron and Zn/Cu slides. Pointer only: the energy side (why that charge is favoured) is Unit 3, U3.4 and U3.7; do not teach ionization energy. Charges are written plain and large (3−, 2−, 1−) because the superscript minus is faint.

fields.headline: Example: Predict the Ions of Mg, Al, S, Br
fields.subhead: We do this one together. Copy the setup, not just the answer.
fields.problem: Use valence electrons to predict each ion. Give the move, the result, and the charge.
fields.g1_b:
Mg: group 2
Al: group 13
S: group 16
Br: group 17
fields.g2_b:
Valence electrons
Lose or gain how many
Noble gas and charge
fields.mustwrite: Lose or gain the fewest electrons to reach 8 valence electrons.

imageSubjects.aside: four sample vials of magnesium, aluminum, sulfur, and bromine on a dark bench

slides.notes: NEW worked example (replaces the earlier Mg2+/S2- configuration example, which this one subsumes). Do together; work area empty on purpose. Answers on next slide. Image slot empty. Prompt subject: four sample vials of magnesium, aluminum, sulfur, and bromine on a dark bench.

fields.headline: Mg, Al, S, and Br Ions, Worked
fields.subhead: Count, move, result, charge. Check the electron count at the end.
fields.f1_b:
Each line reads: valence,
move, noble gas, charge.
fields.work:
Mg: 2, lose 2, [Ne], 2+
Al: 3, lose 3, [Ne], 3+
S: 6, gain 2, [Ar], 2−
Br: 7, gain 1, [Kr], 1−
fields.mustwrite: Mg 2+, Al 3+, S 2−, Br 1−. Each move ends at a noble gas configuration.

slides.notes: Mg: 12 e to 10, Mg2+, [Ne]. Al: 13 to 10, Al3+, [Ne]. S: 16 to 18, S2-, [Ar]. Br: 35 to 36, Br-, [Kr] (3d10 already full). All numbers re-added in the figure script assertions. Anion charges are written plain (2−, 1−) on the slide for legibility. Same pattern, same rule: Mg2+ and S2- were the old example's ions. The picture slot holds a click build for S only (two down arrows added); Mg, Al and Br stay in the text.

fields.headline: Check Yourself
fields.subhead: Work these in your notes. We compare in a minute.
fields.s1_b: Valence electrons in Al, Se, and Xe?
fields.s2_b: Write it. Name the matching noble gas.
fields.s3_b: Predict O's ion. Write its full configuration.
fields.s4_b: [Ar] shorthand for Fe^{3+}, Cu^{2+}, and Zn^{2+}.

imageSubjects.band: a periodic table wall chart photographed at a shallow angle

slides.notes: Answers. 1) Al 3, Se 6, Xe 8. 2) Ca2+: 20 to 18 electrons, 1s2 2s2 2p6 3s2 3p6 = [Ar], argon. 3) O: group 16, 6 valence, gain 2, O2- (charge 2−), 10 electrons, 1s2 2s2 2p6 = [Ne]. 4) Fe3+: [Ar] 3d5; the two 4s electrons leave first, then one 3d. (The 'which leave first' part is not printed on the tile.) 5) Cu2+ [Ar] 3d9 (27 e); Zn2+ [Ar] 3d10 (28 e). The slide tile 4 carries Fe3+, Cu2+, Zn2+ together, so items 4 and 5 share one tile. If time, oral extras using the rule: K 1 valence, lose 1, K+, [Ar]; Se 6 valence, gain 2, Se2-, [Kr]; Al 3 valence, lose 3, Al3+, [Ne]. Group 14 (Si, C) and transition metals: not predicted by the rule here (PROVISIONAL). Tile 3 was changed from 'write the O2- configuration' to a predict-then-write prompt so the new rule is checked.
